chunks: Choosing the PCB layer count. The question: How to choose how many layers for PCB?
Layer count is the number of copper layers in a circuit board.
You choose it from what the board must do: how dense its connections are, how fast its signals switch, how much power it carries, and what it may cost.
Start with two layers and add more only when you can name a specific reason.
Think of a road network. Two roads that cross need a bridge. A big interchange stacks several levels of overpasses so everything gets through, but each level costs a lot.
Board layers work the same way: more layers give room for crossing connections, but each pair adds cost.
The analogy breaks in one place: extra layers also add solid ground sheets that make fast signals cleaner, which has no road equivalent.
Top view of BGA pads (circles).
The outer rows can leave on the top layer, but the channels between pads hold only one trace, so deeper rows must drop through vias onto inner signal layers.
That is where layer count comes from.
BGA (ball grid array): a chip with a grid of solder balls underneath instead of pins on its edges. Pitch: the center-to-center distance between neighboring balls.
Escape routing: getting every signal out from under a dense chip ("Components that need more PCB layers"). Via: a plated hole that carries a signal to another layer.
Its round copper pad takes up space. Plane: a whole layer of solid copper used for ground or power ("Which layers should be ground", "Which layers for power planes").
Take a BGA with a 16 by 16 grid of balls at 0. 8 mm pitch. Each via pad is 0. 45 mm across, so the gap between pads is 0. 8 - 0. 45 = 0. 35 mm. A 0. 1 mm trace with 0.
1 mm clearance on each side needs 0. 30 mm, so one trace fits through each gap, but not two. That lets each layer bring out about two rows of balls.
Of the 8 rows from edge to center, the middle 6 by 6 balls are power and ground, so 5 rows carry signals.
That needs 3 signal layers, plus 2 planes, and boards come in even counts, so 6 layers. That is the whole idea.
"I'd choose the fewest layers that satisfy routing, signal integrity and EMI, and I'd name the reason for each layer.
Dense BGAs drive signal layers, about two rows of balls per layer.
Fast edges or controlled impedance need an adjacent ground plane, so I'd go to four layers: signal, ground, power, signal. Multiple rails, DDR or SerDes push me to six or eight.
Cost goes up with each pair, so I only add layers when something won't route or won't pass EMC."
